headline: High: ECC’s writable, networked workspace can conflict with and ingest outputs from the content-writing agent, creating default-path prompt injection, leakage, and cascading-error risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is a content-writing agent with broad network egress, while agent B has stdin/stdout, MCP, filesystem, and browser surfaces plus a workflow that uses skills and session files. That creates a plausible path for A-generated content to be copied into B’s trusted inputs or files. The pairwise interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes upward from low.
conditions: IF agent A output is copied into agent B session files or MCP inputs without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF agent B treats file or stdin content as instructions, attacker-controlled text can steer tool use.
mitigations: Add a provenance banner to all A outputs before B ingests them.
Disable automatic parsing of A-generated text as commands in B.
Route A→B handoff through a plain-text review step.
requires-engineering: add content provenance tags to shared files.
requires-engineering: enforce allowlisted instruction schemas for B inputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: B explicitly reads and writes filesystem locations, handles session summaries, hooks, and security findings, and can use network egress to APIs. A has broad network egress and is a content-writing agent, so if they share a workspace or files, sensitive material can flow from B into A’s outputs or external destinations. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so this remains inferred.
conditions: IF A and B share any filesystem or session directory, B-managed data can be exposed through A’s network egress.
IF B writes secrets or findings into files that A reads, those contents can be summarized or transmitted externally.
mitigations: Separate A and B workspaces and home directories.
Remove secrets from shared files before A reads them.
Turn off A network access for sensitive runs.
Review B session files for sensitive data before reuse.
requires-engineering: add per-directory access controls and redaction hooks.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: B can execute shell, modify git state, write the filesystem, and spawn subprocesses; A is a content-writing agent with broad network egress. If both operate on the same repo or directory, concurrent writes and git mutations can overwrite each other or corrupt state. The profiles show no locking or isolation mechanism, so the safer choice is high rather than medium.
conditions: IF A and B target the same working tree, git history or files can be overwritten.
IF B runs multiple instances without separate roots, session files can collide.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories to A and B.
Pause one agent before the other writes git state.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
Check for file collisions before commits.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable paths.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B’s workflow surface emphasizes skills and subagents, and it can act on files, git, and browsers; A produces content that B may consume. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into commits, browser actions, or generated artifacts. No verification step is documented, so the interaction is plausible in default use but not proven.
conditions: IF B uses A output as source material without verification, factual errors can propagate.
IF B converts A text into commits or browser actions, downstream mistakes become persistent.
mitigations: Require a human review of A outputs before B acts on them.
Add a verification checklist for facts cited by A.
Limit B to read-only mode when consuming A content.
Log A→B handoffs for audit.
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking before actions.

E_compliance.rationale: B explicitly handles session summaries, hooks, agent definitions, security findings, and retention settings, while A has broad network egress and is unverified docs-only content. If regulated or sensitive data enters B’s files and A can transmit or summarize it externally, retention or residency obligations can be violated. The profiles do not specify a concrete jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in B session files or hooks, retention and access controls must be enforced.
IF A is used to transmit content derived from B’s sensitive files, external disclosure obligations may be triggered.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of B session files.
Set short retention for B artifacts.
Review A outputs before external sharing.
Document data-class handling rules for both agents.
requires-engineering: add residency and retention policy enforcement.
